newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia stocks up, U.S. analyst says steer clear.
newsitem.headline: Colombia stocks up, U.S. analyst says steer clear.

text.p: Colombian shares edged marginally up for the second day led by demand for cement maufacturer Cementos Caribe and brewing giant Bavaria.

U.S. analysts Smith Barney Research advised investors to steer clear of the market, which started off as one of the hottest in the world, until issues such as the U.S. decision whether to decertify the country as a drug war ally for the second year and possible economic sanctions are resolved.
Bogota's IBB index gained 0.7 percent to close at 966.5 on volume of 830 million pesos. Medellin's IBOMED index ended up 0.1 percent at 14,794.5 on 940 million pesos.
"Trading was light today and there was only demand from foreign funds in a few isolated cases such as Cementos Caribe and Bavaria," a Bogota broker said.

Bavaria gained 3.92 percent to close at 5,820 in Bogota and rose 4.02 percent to 5,825 in Medellin. Cementos Caribe rose 1.01 percent to 5,000 in Bogota, but was not traded in Medellin. Banco de Colombia fell 0.7 percent to 425 pesos on the Bogota exchange and dropped 1.16 percent in Medellin.
Smith Barney Research said congressional sessions in February to debate tougher sentences for drug crimes were the last chance for Colombia to save itself from decertification.

"We do not recommend entry into the Colombian market until the decertification overhang is gone. Failure to pass the bills would insure equities will have a poor environment for at least two months. A longer term outlook would hinge more on economic fundamentals and the fiscal deficit outlook," the organization said.

Independent economic think-tank Fedesarrollo published a report Thursday that indicated large and medium-sized businesses were gloomy about the outlook and skeptical of the effects of the recently declared state of economic emergency.
Of 129 companies surveyed, 95.3 percent said they thought the economic emergency measures, designed to rein in a yawning fiscal deficit and stem the tide of dollars flowing into Colombia, were bad.
More than 90 percent said they were pessimistic about current economic policy and believed it generated instability.
